t.1.62.1: When a full thousand years had passed, all the gods came to the great sage, who had bathed at the completion of his vow, wishing to bestow on him the fruit of his austerities.
t.1.62.2: Brahmā, of exceedingly great splendour, spoke these most pleasing words: "You are a ṛṣi through the auspicious deeds you have earned by your own effort; may good fortune be yours."
t.1.62.3: Having spoken thus to him, the lord of the gods returned again to heaven. Viśvāmitra, of great splendor, once more performed great austerities.
t.1.62.4: Then, after a long time had passed, O best of men, Menakā, the foremost of apsarases, came to bathe in the lakes of Puṣkara.
t.1.62.5: There the greatly radiant son of Kuśika saw Menakā, peerless in beauty, like a flash of lightning in a rain-cloud.
t.1.62.6: Seeing her, the sage, fallen under the sway of Kandarpa, said this to her: "O Apsaras, may you be welcome; dwell here in my hermitage. Bestow your favour on me, who am utterly bewildered by Madana; may good fortune be yours."
t.1.62.7: Thus addressed, that lovely-hipped woman then took up her dwelling there; for indeed a great obstacle to his austerity had come upon Viśvāmitra.
t.1.62.8: O gentle Rāghava, while she dwelt in Viśvāmitra's hermitage, five years and five more passed by happily.
t.1.62.9: Then, when that time had passed, the great sage Viśvāmitra became as though ashamed, wholly given over to anxious thought and sorrow.
t.1.62.10: O Raghunandana, a thought filled with indignation arose in the sage: “All this is the work of the gods, a great theft of my austerity.”
t.1.62.11: Ten years have passed as though they were but a single day and night; this obstacle has arisen for me, overpowered as I was by desire and delusion.
t.1.62.12: Sighing deeply, the best of sages was afterwards stricken with grief through remorse.
t.1.62.13: Seeing the apsaras Menakā standing frightened and trembling, her palms joined in supplication, Viśvāmitra, the son of Kuśika, dismissed her with gentle words and went to the northern mountain, O Rāma.
t.1.62.14: That greatly renowned one, having made a firm and unwavering resolve and desiring to conquer, reached the bank of the Kauśikī and performed exceedingly terrible austerities.
t.1.62.15: O Rāma, while he practiced fierce austerity on the northern mountain for a thousand years, fear arose among the gods.
t.1.62.16: All the gods, together with the hosts of seers, assembled and took counsel: "It is well; let this son of Kuśika obtain the title of great seer."
t.1.62.17: Having heard the words of the deities, the Grandfather of all the worlds spoke sweet words to Viśvāmitra, whose wealth was his austerity.
t.1.62.19: Having heard the words of Brahmā, Viśvāmitra, whose wealth was his austerity, joined his palms in reverence, bowed low, and replied to the Grandfather.
t.1.62.18: Welcome, great sage, my child! Pleased by your fierce austerity, I grant you greatness and foremost rank among the sages, O Kauśika.
t.1.62.20: If the Lord confers upon me the incomparable title of brahmarṣi, won through my own auspicious deeds, then I shall be one who has conquered his senses.
t.1.62.21: Then Brahmā said to him, "You have not yet conquered your senses; strive on, O tiger among sages." Having spoken thus, he went to heaven.
t.1.62.22: When the gods had departed, the great sage Viśvāmitra, arms raised aloft, without support and subsisting on air alone, went on practicing austerities.
t.1.62.24: Thus for a thousand years he undertook fierce austerity. But while that great sage Viśvāmitra was performing his austerities,
t.1.62.23: Steadfast in dharma, the ascetic whose wealth was austerity practiced the penance of the five fires; in the rainy season he took the open sky as his only shelter, and in the cold season he stood in water through nights and days.
t.1.62.26: He spoke words that were beneficial to himself but harmful to Kauśika.
t.1.62.25: Very great was the agitation of the gods and of Vāsava; then Śakra, together with all the hosts of the Maruts, addressed the apsaras Rambhā.
